title: Holy, Holy, Holy: Isaiah's Vision and Call
summary: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned in the temple, surrounded by seraphim who call to one another that he is holy, holy, holy. Overwhelmed by his own uncleanness, Isaiah cries out, and a seraph touches his lips with a burning coal to atone for his sin. When the Lord asks whom he should send, Isaiah volunteers, and is given a hard commission: to preach to a people who will not listen, until the land lies desolate and only a holy stump remains.
story: The book has already shown Judah's rebellion (chapter 1), its pride and idolatry (chapters 2 to 3), and the sour fruit of the vineyard (chapter 5). Now, instead of opening with his call as Jeremiah and Ezekiel do, Isaiah tells it here, perhaps to show where his message came from and why it is so severe. The vision of God's holiness explains the book's favorite title for God, the Holy One of Israel, and the commission explains why Isaiah's preaching will mostly harden rather than heal. The chapter also prepares for the next section (chapters 7 to 12), where Isaiah meets King Ahaz and a people who refuse to listen, and where hope rests with a remnant and a coming king.
historical:
King Uzziah (also called Azariah) reigned over Judah for about fifty-two years (2 Kings 15:2) and died around 740 BC; scholars' dates for his death range from about 742 to 734 BC. His reign was one of Judah's most prosperous, but 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 records that in pride he entered the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for priests, and was struck with a skin disease that kept him isolated until his death. Isaiah's vision of the true King in the temple, set in the year the proud earthly king died, is surely meant to be read against that background.

Uzziah's death came as Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III was beginning its westward campaigns. Within a few years Judah would face invasion from Aram and Israel (chapter 7), and within twenty years the northern kingdom would be destroyed. The desolation described in verses 11 to 13 unfolded over the next century and a half, culminating in the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC.
cultural:
Jerusalem's temple, built by Solomon, had an inner room, the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood beneath two golden cherubim. The ark was understood as God's footstool and the cherubim as his throne. Isaiah sees what the temple represented: the Lord enthroned, so vast that only the hem of his robe fills the building. Kings in the ancient Near East wore long robes as a mark of status, and a longer train meant greater majesty.

The seraphim appear by that name only here in the Bible. The word means burning ones, and the same word is used for the fiery serpents in the wilderness (Numbers 21:6-8). Some scholars compare them to the winged serpent figures common in Egyptian and Judean royal art of the period. Whatever their form, they cover their faces (they cannot look on God) and their feet (possibly a modest way of referring to the body), and they sing. The altar from which the coal is taken is probably the incense altar that stood before the inner room. In Israel's worship, unclean lips were a serious matter: uncleanness barred a person from God's presence, and Isaiah has seen the King.
literary: The chapter is a first-person narrative of a vision, and it follows a pattern also found in the calls of Moses, Gideon, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel: an encounter with God, an objection or sense of unworthiness, reassurance, and a commission. Isaiah's version has a striking scene of heavenly council, where the Lord asks, “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” (compare 1 Kings 22:19-22, where the prophet Micaiah sees the Lord consulting his heavenly host). The threefold holy is the Hebrew way of expressing the superlative: God is utterly holy. The commission in verses 9 and 10 is built as a chiasm (a mirrored pattern): heart, ears, eyes, then eyes, ears, heart. The chapter ends not in despair but with a single line of hope, the holy seed in the stump.

outline.t: The Lord on his throne and the song of the seraphim
The commission to a people who will not hear
How long? Until the land is desolate, and a holy stump

doctrines.note: The seraphim's song is the Bible's most famous statement of God's holiness: his utter otherness, majesty, and moral purity. The whole earth is full of his glory, yet his holiness exposes even a prophet's uncleanness.
Isaiah's sin is removed by a coal from the altar, the place of sacrifice. God himself provides the means of cleansing; Isaiah contributes nothing but his confession.
Only after he is cleansed does Isaiah volunteer to be sent. His commission is hard, and it shows that faithfulness in God's mission is measured by obedience, not by visible results.
The hardening of verses 9 and 10 is itself a judgment: a people who have long refused to listen will be confirmed in their refusal. Yet even this judgment preserves a holy seed.

words.note: Qadosh, holy, sung three times in verse 3. The root idea is separateness: what is holy belongs to God and is set apart from common use. When applied to God himself it means he is in a class of his own, above and beyond all creatures, and morally pure. From this vision Isaiah takes his name for God, the Holy One of Israel.

Saraph, seraph, from a root meaning to burn. Outside this chapter the word describes fiery serpents (Numbers 21:6; Isaiah 14:29; 30:6). Here it names heavenly beings who attend God's throne. Their fiery nature suits the purifying coal one of them brings.

Kaphar, to atone or cover, the verb used for the sacrifices of Leviticus and the Day of Atonement. In verse 7 Isaiah's sin is atoned for. The same word will be central to how the church understands Christ's sacrifice.

christ: The New Testament draws on this chapter in two important ways. First, John 12:37-41 quotes both Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10 and then says that Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory and spoke of him. John understands the King whom Isaiah saw as including the Son, which is why Christians have long read the threefold holy in light of the Trinity, though the Hebrew form is primarily a superlative. Second, Jesus and the apostles quote verses 9 and 10 to explain why many in Israel did not believe (Matthew 13:14-15; Mark 4:12; Acts 28:25-27). Revelation 4:8 echoes the song of the seraphim in the worship of heaven. Isaiah's cleansing by a coal from the altar also foreshadows the greater cleansing Christ provides by his own sacrifice.

hard.q: Why would God send a prophet to make people's hearts dull so that they will not turn and be healed?
hard.a: Verses 9 and 10 are among the hardest words in the prophets. Several responses are offered. Many interpreters read the commands as ironic or as describing the result of Isaiah's preaching rather than its intent: his faithful message will in fact harden a people who have already refused God, just as the sun that melts wax hardens clay. Others emphasize that this is judicial hardening, a judgment on those who have long resisted, not the hardening of the innocent; in Exodus, Pharaoh's hardening is described both as his own act and as God's. The hardening is also limited: Isaiah asks how long, and the answer implies an end, and the chapter closes with a holy seed. The New Testament uses the passage the same way, to explain unbelief while still preaching and inviting (Acts 28:25-31), and Paul argues that Israel's hardening is partial and temporary (Romans 11:25-26). The passage does not remove the mystery of how God's sovereignty and human responsibility meet, but it places hardening within judgment and within a purpose that includes mercy.

questions: Isaiah's first response to God's holiness is to see his own sin. What happens to a person's confidence and humility when they catch a glimpse of who God is?
Isaiah volunteered before he knew how hard his assignment would be. What does it mean to say yes to God without knowing the outcome?
How do you respond to the idea that faithfulness may not bring visible success?
